Article Title: Neeraj Chopra’s 2026 season over after ankle ligament tear, Diamond League Final and Asian Games ruled out
Article Text:
Neeraj Chopra (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s javelin star Neeraj Chopra ’s 2026 season has come to a premature end after the Olympic and world champion suffered a ligament tear in his ankle during training, ruling him out of next month’s Diamond League Final and Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.Chopra made the announcement on Saturday, revealing that the injury occurred shortly after he produced a season’s best throw at the Lausanne Diamond League. Following consultations with his doctor and support team, the 28-year-old decided against taking any further competitive risk and will now focus on rehabilitation.The setback comes at a particularly frustrating juncture for Chopra, who had begun to feel that he was finally rediscovering the consistency and momentum he had been searching for this season.“After a period of hard work, I finally felt I was gaining the momentum I had been looking for with a Season’s Best throw in Lausanne,” Chopra said in a statement. “Unfortunately, shortly after, I sustained a ligament tear in my ankle during training. After discussions with my doctor and team, we’ve decided that I will sit out the rest of this season.“It’s disappointing, especially because I felt close to finding my rhythm.But as they say, setbacks are a part of the journey.“My focus now is on recovering well and coming back even stronger.”The injury means Chopra will miss the Asian Games, where he was expected to spearhead India’s medal campaign in athletics. His absence will be a major setback for the country’s hopes at the continental showpiece, which begins next month in Japan.Chopra’s 2026 campaign had been a mixed one. He returned to competition at the Doha Diamond League in June following a lengthy injury layoff and finished fourth with a throw of 85.69m. He then won silver in Glasgow with an 85.83m effort, although Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Pathirage stole the spotlight by clinching gold with a huge 89.75m throw.The Lausanne Diamond League was Chopra’s third competitive appearance of the season and had offered signs that he was moving closer to his best. His season’s-best effort there had provided a much-needed confidence boost and was expected to serve as an important build-up to the Asian Games.Instead, Lausanne has turned out to be his final competition of the year.Chopra will also miss the Diamond League Final. He had moved up to seventh in the qualification standings and remained in contention for a place in the season-ending event, but the ankle injury has now brought his campaign to a halt.For Chopra, the priority is now clear: recover fully, avoid rushing his comeback and return to competition at full strength.For India, however, his absence leaves a significant void heading into the Asian Games, where the defending Olympic champion was expected to be one of the country’s biggest medal hopes.
Article Summary: Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra suffers ligament tear in his ankle. Chopra will miss the Diamond League Final and Asian Games in Japan. The 28-year- old says he will now focus on rehabilitation. The setback comes at a particularly frustrating juncture for Chopra.

Ryan Williams arrived in India as an Australian footballer looking for a new challenge. Three years later, the Bengaluru FC winger has become one of the Indian national team's most vocal advocates, embracing both the club and the country as home.The 32-year-old has experienced near misses with Bengaluru FC, adapting to Indian football, and the responsibility of mentoring younger players while representing India. Despite a six-year trophy drought at the Sree Kanteerava Stadium, he believes the club is closer to success than results suggest.In this conversation with TimesofIndia.com, Williams, who was roped in by JSW Sports recently, speaks about Bengaluru FC's title ambitions, manager Pep Muñoz's philosophy, the OCI debate, national team pride, and why life in Bengaluru has been an enjoyable chapter of his career.Yeah, probably the last three years of my career has been the most, first and foremost, transformative, I would say, definitely. But also the one I've enjoyed the most with kind of what I'm doing with BFC, although we haven't won anything.My everyday life here, I love it. I love living in Bangalore, the football club itself, the way the club is run.Then obviously moving on to the national team has been such an amazing experience for me. It's one that has been so positive and hopefully I can continue to keep it in a positive way and just try and help the younger boys, try and, if possible, get more players like me to do what I've done, for me to show them it is possible. I've said in many interviews that if there is anything I can do, please reach out. And I've had boys reach out, which is good because obviously the reason I'm here is to help Indian football at the end of the day.Not at all. I don't think so at all. I think it's more the fans who have been here to enjoy the super successful times. We have been slowly building and almost got there. The season before I came, they got to three finals. And then the season after, we had a managerial change. Then the season after that, we got to the ISL Cup final. And from our own doing, we couldn't hold out.Obviously last season, with it being a truncated season, just when we kind of found our feet, the season finished. So this season will be really exciting. I don't feel any pressure personally.The fans are amazing. They obviously stick with us through the good and the bad. They're probably the best fans in India in terms of how they do stick behind us when things aren't going so well. So for us, it's more about trying to give them something back. That's how I see it, because they've been so amazing with us, especially with me having come over here from Australia and everything that's come in between.The hardest thing to do as a men's professional footballer is to win trophies. And that's something that, you know, the last three seasons we haven't done since I've been here. So it's definitely something that we've spoken about and something that we want to put right.I'm a pretty well-travelled guy. I moved to the UK by myself when I was 16, moved in with a foster family, had to figure all that out by myself and then back to Australia and then India. So it was difficult the kind of first six to eight weeks in terms of outside of football. But then after that, I kind of found my feet and understood how things worked.And there's still things that I'm not quite 100 percent on, but, you know, I've got a good network of people supporting me, which definitely helped. And then in terms of football, I think any new club you go to, especially a different country as well. I mean, I look back on my first season and towards the end, I started to come through and started to be more confident and got used to the players I'm with, got used to the surroundings, the pitches, even the day to day.I would say one thing that helped me on the pitch was having Simon Grayson (Bengaluru FC manager from 2022 until 23) and his management staff because they were all English and they took the sessions and organised everything the way that I was used to for 12 years in England. So that was a massive help for me. But it did take me the first half of the season to really find my feet and then started to enjoy my football at the end.And then I just kind of kept going, kept believing in myself and got used to (it). Because the European players are obviously different to Indian players and there's positives and negatives about both. So it's trying to work out how do I communicate in a proper way. They all do speak English, that's not the issue. In the UK, you can kind of shout and scream at people and they listen to the message and not how the message is given. Whereas here you have to be more cautious about how you give the message rather than what the message is sometimes. And that's one thing I've been trying to help the young boys with. Just trying to be more positive around them and let them that I'm here to support you. We're both on the same team. We're trying to go for the same thing. So it's in my best interest to help them perform at their maximum capability. In turn, if we win something because of him, everybody wins. So that was one thing that I had to kind of figure out in the first six months.I really like it. I was lucky enough to work with Gerard (Zaragoza) and Sebas (Sebastian Vega) before who have a similar approach... the Spanish management style, which I was new to at first when Gerard came in. So it's put me in good stead because we spent a year and a half or thereabouts together.And last season was good in a way that he [Muñoz] came in. He came in with his coaching staff and it was really good because everybody got to kind of figure out how to work with each other, what exactly he wants to do on the pitch. And that's put us in good stead for this season because last season was, for lack of better words, almost like a draft copy. It was like a dummy run. So now we've been in pre-season early, we're spending a lot more time on the pitch, figuring out exactly what he wants and how we can best do that on the pitch to obviously give us results, put people in positions that works best for everybody. So I'm really excited.I really love what he's doing on the football pitch. And the good thing is that obviously that small part we had with him last season has been, like I said, a dummy run to push us forward into this season. So we don't need as much time together on the grass to connect the dots. The dots are connected and now it's just about fine tuning it and pushing it forward.I think for Indian football, for it to grow at a faster rate than what it is now, we need to see success in the national team. And if that means that the Sports Passport and the OCI can help us in the next one to two years to push us up higher up the rankings and get us qualified for Asian Cups and stuff like that, then there's going to be more interest in Indian football. That's great, but I think long term, I think it would work. I think if we can send the younger boys from here that way, rather than bringing them this way, if that makes sense.If they're looking at just coming here when it [national team] does good, I think maybe they're the wrong kind of people we're looking for. I think we want players that want to come here, give everything for the country and help the national team. And within helping the national team, we actually help the whole ecosystem. So, you know, like for me, there was no guarantees of anything. I have kind of done it because that's what I wanted to do. I'm proud to play for India. There has to be that pride.We want people that wear the jersey with pride and are willing to give everything to play for the country. I think that's what it means to play for your country.There's no city that I've lived in that's like Bengaluru. You know, it is in itself its own kind of country, if you will. Like, first of all, I love the weather. The weather is perfect. If you came straight from the UK, you're in heaven because you have these nice periods where it's nice and cool, like it is now in the rain.And then in the summer, it's nice and warm, but not too hot.You know, the kind of the restaurants here, which my wife and I try to go to as much as possible. There's just so much to do. There's so much to see. There's, you know, so many different aspects to this city that make it beautiful and I really love it all.For me, it's a very relaxed lifestyle. And that's kind of how I like to live my life, in a very relaxed, laidback, not taking things too seriously way. And I feel like here's the perfect place.
Article Summary: Ryan Williams joined ISL club Bengaluru FC in 2023. He has played two games for India so far. The 32-year-old has experienced near misses with the club. Despite a six-year trophy drought, he believes the club is closer to success than results suggest.

Article Title: 'An honour to become the first English player': Harry Kane reacts after making history in Germany
Article Text:
Harry Kane after winning Germany's Footballer of the Year award (X - @HKane)

Kane beats teammate Olise

Bayern Munich and England striker Harry Kane has become the first English player to win Germany’s Footballer of the Year award, adding another major honour to his impressive spell in Germany. Kane was presented with the prestigious award at the Allianz Arena ahead of Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga opener. The striker described the recognition as a special moment, particularly after receiving it in front of the club’s supporters.Sharing his reaction on social media, Kane wrote: "An honour to become the first English player to win Germany's Footballer of the Year award. A special feeling to receive it at the Allianz in front of our incredible fans. Great to collect it alongside the gaffer and Giulia Gwinn - congratulations to you both!" England star on X.He also congratulated Bayern coach Vincent Kompany and Giulia Gwinn, who were named Coach of the Year and Women’s Footballer of the Year respectively.Kane was voted the winner by members of the Association of German Sports Journalists (VDS), collecting 272 of 659 votes. Bayern teammate Michael Olise finished second with 203 votes, while Kane succeeds Florian Wirtz, who won the award in 2025.The honour recognises Kane’s outstanding 2025-26 campaign, during which he scored a remarkable 36 Bundesliga goals.The Germany Footballer of the Year prize is Kane’s latest individual achievement. Earlier in the week, he was awarded the European Golden Shoe after finishing as Europe’s leading scorer during the 2025-26 season. He also celebrated team success with Bayern Munich, who defeated Borussia Dortmund 2-1 in the 2026 Franz Beckenbauer Supercup on Saturday.Although Kane did not get on the scoresheet in the Supercup, his remarkable run of individual honours continued with his historic recognition in Germany.
Article Summary: Harry Kane is the first English player to win Germany's Footballer of the Year award. Kane was presented with the award at the Allianz Arena ahead of Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga opener. The striker described the recognition as a special moment, particularly after receiving it in front of the club's supporters.

Article Title: BCCI stance on Sports Bill creates confusion within Board
Article Text:
Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) Secretary Devajit Saikia, left, with BCCI Centre of Excellence (CoE) head VVS Laxman (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: A recent development in a matter concerning the Odisha Cricket Association’s (OCA) elections in the Odisha High Court has created confusion among the Indian cricket board’s ( BCCI ) state units over the National Sports Governance Act, passed in 2025.In an affidavit filed by the BCCI’s legal team and authorised by board secretary Devajit Saikia, it has been claimed that the OCA must conduct its elections as per the existing BCCI constitution, which was amended following the Lodha Committee recommendations in 2019.The BCCI has asserted that cricket is not a ‘designated sport’ even though the Act has been enacted, suggesting its reluctance to come under the ambit of the National Sports Board (NSB).Several state associations were under the impression that fresh elections would remain in abeyance until December 2026, as per the sports ministry’s notice issued last December. The biggest point of friction is the cooling-off period for office-bearers. The Act does not specify any cooling-off period and also relaxes certain areas related to conflict of interest.The incumbent OCA office-bearers have claimed that they are following the government’s directions, while the BCCI has taken an opposite stance.“It is submitted that even though the National Sports Governance Act, 2025 has been enacted, the sport of cricket has not been notified as a ‘designated sport’ for the said National Sports Governance Act, 2025 to apply,” the BCCI’s affidavit stated.“That Odisha Cricket Association has similar provisions of no office-bearer continuing for more than two terms consecutively, it is imperative that timely elections should be held in order to avoid continuation of any person for more than two terms consecutively and to uphold the spirit of the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court,” the affidavit, a copy of which is with TOI, read.The next hearing is scheduled for September 1.Interestingly, during a parliamentary discussion in August 2025, Vijayawada MP and Andhra Cricket Association president Kesineni Sivanath welcomed the bill and stated that the BCCI already adheres to its core principles.It was mentioned that the government had only exempted the BCCI from coming under the ambit of the Right to Information (RTI) Act since it did not depend on public funds. In May, the Central Information Commission, while exempting the BCCI from the RTI Act, stated that the Lodha Committee’s recommendations were only ‘advisory in nature’.The BCCI’s recent stance has created an ambiguous situation within the board.“If the government has notified that sports bodies can defer elections till December 2026, every state unit would believe it can wait until then before holding elections for select posts. The power forces in BCCI have always advocated the importance of continuity in administration. The board’s reluctance to adhere to government directives can disrupt it just when the new office-bearers were gaining experience.“It has also created confusion over the governance of the sport. The state bodies need to know if they have to follow the Sports Governance Act or the BCCI constitution,” a senior official told TOI.The BCCI held its elections last September, before the sports ministry issued its advisory. BCCI vice-president Rajiv Shukla will complete six years in office next year, while secretary Saikia is into his second term as an office-bearer and will complete six years in 2028 before entering the cooling-off period under the BCCI constitution.If the BCCI eventually comes under the ambit of the NSB, the mandatory cooling-off period would not apply to its office-bearers.
Article Summary: Odisha Cricket Association's (OCA) elections in the Odisha High Court has created confusion among the Indian cricket board’s ( BCCI ) state units over the National Sports Governance Act, passed in 2025. The Act does not specify any cooling-off period and also relaxes certain areas related to conflict of interest. The incumbent OCA office-bearers have claimed that they are following the government's directions.

Article Title: Hockey World Cup: Belgium break Indian hearts in shootout as Harmanpreet’s side finishes eighth
Article Text:
Belgium beat India (AP Photo)

Belgium strike again, India refuse to give up

Shootout drama ends India's hopes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s spirited fightback ended in heartbreak as Belgium prevailed in a tense penalty shootout after the two sides played out a thrilling 3-3 draw in regulation time. India had made the brighter start and took the lead through Abhishek, whose sixth-minute field goal gave the hosts a 1-0 advantage. Belgium responded with sustained pressure, earning multiple penalty corners, but India’s defence held firm.The match changed dramatically in the second quarter. Roman Duvekot restored parity for Belgium with a close-range finish before Hugo Labouchere put them ahead with a powerful drag-flick from a penalty corner. Belgium went into half-time 2-1 up.India came out strongly after the break and levelled through captain Harmanpreet Singh , who converted a penalty corner with a superb drag-flick in the 31st minute. Belgium challenged the goal with a review, but the decision went India's way.The third quarter remained fiercely contested, with Belgium applying pressure and India creating opportunities of their own. Despite Belgium enjoying more possession, India held their shape to take the scores level at 2-2 into the final quarter.Belgium regained the lead in the 47th minute when Nicolas de Kerpel fired home a field goal.The goal was referred for a possible obstruction, but the original decision was upheld and Belgium moved 3-2 ahead. India were dealt another blow when veteran Manpreet Singh took a stick to the face and left the field for medical attention.With time running out, India pulled their goalkeeper in favour of an additional outfield player and threw numbers forward in search of an equaliser. Their gamble paid off in dramatic fashion.Harmanpreet struck again in the 60th minute, finding the target to make it 3-3 and force a penalty shootout.The shootout began disastrously for India. Harmanpreet's first attempt was saved by Belgium goalkeeper Vincent Vanasch after the Indian captain appeared to stop while expecting a whistle. Belgium converted their opening attempt, while Vanasch then denied Sukhjeet Singh as well.India eventually found their rhythm. Shilanand Lakra opened India's account before Belgium restored their advantage. Dilpreet Singh then converted to bring the shootout level at 2-2.Belgium regained the lead through a penalty stroke after Mohith was penalised for a foul on Van Dessel, with Hendrickx converting. India stayed alive when Abhishek scored to make it 3-3.The decisive moment came when Duvekot found the target for Belgium. India took a referral in an attempt to overturn the decision, but the call stood.Belgium therefore won the shootout and ended India's brave fight after an extraordinary contest and they finish 8th in this World Cup.
Article Summary: India's spirited fightback ended in heartbreak as Belgium prevailed in a tense penalty shootout after the two sides played out a thrilling 3-3 draw in regulation time. India had made the brighter start and took the lead through Abhishek, whose sixth-minute field goal gave the hosts a 1-0 advantage. Roman Duvekot restored parity for Belgium with a close-range finish before Hugo Labouchere put them ahead with a powerful drag-flick from a penalty corner.

Article Title: Praggnanandhaa’s golden summer: From Norway Chess glory to GCT crown
Article Text:
Indian Grandmaster Praggnanandhaa

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Until this summer, no Indian had won the elite Norway Chess title. There was no Indian name alongside the Grand Chess Tour finale either. R Praggnanandhaa, that shy and super-sharp boy from Chennai, a Viswanathan Anand mentee like many from the city, now has both crowns to call his own.Late on Thursday, Praggnanandhaa, the world No. 12, claimed the Grand Chess Tour (GCT) title, beating Fabiano Caruana 15-13 in St Louis, US, considered the new Linares in chess circles, and pocketed $200,000 in prize money. Praggnanandhaa thus became the first Indian and only the seventh player in the tournament’s 11-year history to achieve the feat.It won’t be an exaggeration to call him the ‘unofficial’ Total Chess world champion ahead of the tournament’s inauguration next year and the pilot project later this year in Budapest.The 21-year-old has chosen to play next month’s Olympiad over the lucrative Global Chess League in Bengaluru. That decision has worked out very well for him because he achieved a major success well in time for the Olympiad, where India will try to defend their maiden team gold medal in three weeks’ time.The positive tidings for Indian chess don’t seem to end. The crop is fearless and the results are relentless, more importantly, at the ‘above Elo 2600’ level and not just below it or in the many online versions of the sport.Earlier this year, Praggnanandhaa had done the unthinkable by beating world No. 1 Magnus Carlsen twice in classical games at Norway Chess, a feat that included an unprecedented sequence of four straight classical wins at the end of the tournament in Oslo.If the Indian chess sun was shining brightly then, it has now just extended its rays to a new region.Praggnanandhaa has shown year-round consistency by topping the GCT table, with only the top four making it to the finale. And then, despite losing the first classical game of the final to Caruana in the title clash and messing up a probable equaliser in the second classical game, worth six points, he still displayed admirable mental strength.Praggnanandhaa won both rapid games, worth four points each, to take the lead over the highly regarded Caruana before drawing the four-game blitz section 4-4, with one win for either player. He had beaten German super talent Vincent Keymer in the semifinals.While this may be subjective, and the chess world has its favourites, experts consider Praggnanandhaa a more well-rounded Indian player than world champion Gukesh and former Elo 2800 member Arjun Erigaisi, partly due to his technical prowess and more universal style of play.That is why his failed campaigns at the 2024 and 2026 Candidates, and the manner in which he imploded, were particularly disheartening for Indian fans.Praggnanandhaa’s St Louis schedule was gruelling. He played 27 rapid and blitz games, then nine classical games, and another 16 games in the semifinals and finals of the Tour.Now, he can rest with a sense of achievement, a high like no other.When his sister Vaishali was not doing too well at the Classical Cairns Cup for women, being played concurrently at the same venue, Praggnanandhaa was plotting his own grand prize. The roles were reversed at the Cyprus Candidates earlier this year when Vaishali won the women’s title and Praggnanandhaa finished seventh in the eight-player field.Not that Praggnanandhaa hadn’t proved himself before at the elite level. He burst into the limelight by reaching the 2023 World Cup final in Baku, the birthplace of the great Garry Kasparov, in Azerbaijan, and has now stamped his authority on the GCT Tour, which has been the brainchild of the Russian.In between his knockout World Cup run and the Norway title, he had several high points. But those came largely in the classical section, with triumphs at Wijk aan Zee, the GCT Romania leg and the UzChess Cup in 2025, all in classical chess.World championship challenger Javokhir Sindarov had humbled Praggnanandhaa twice at the Cyprus Candidates. The Indian avenged those defeats at the Sinquefield Cup, where he finished joint first.Keymer defeated Praggnanandhaa at Sinquefield before getting knocked out by the Indian’s cerebral powers in the semifinals of the Tour Finale.
Article Summary: Praggnanandhaa, the world No. 12, claimed the Grand Chess Tour title, beating Fabiano Caruana 15-13 in St Louis, US. The 21-year-old has chosen to play next month’s Olympiad over the lucrative Global Chess League in Bengaluru.

Article Title: Rumesh Pathirage raises bar again, Neeraj Chopra braces for another test
Article Text:
Neeraj Chopra

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage's sensational season has entered another gear, and for India's Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra , the road to the Diamond League Final and Asian Games now comes with an unmistakable warning.The Sri Lankan javelin star produced a breathtaking 92.07m in Zurich on Thursday to underline why he has become the man to beat this season. It was his second throw beyond 92m in 2026, following his world-leading 92.62m national record in Rome in June.The Zurich effort also pushed Pathirage into rare company. He is only the fourth javelin thrower in history to cross the 92m mark twice, joining legendary names such as Jan Zelezny, Johannes Vetter and Aki Parviainen.Pathirage had to work his way into the competition in Zurich. He opened with 81.50m, improved to 88.23m in the second round and reached 89.90m in the third. After 84.91m in the fourth round and a foul in the fifth, he delivered the knockout blow in the last throw.Former world champion Anderson Peters came second with a season-best 86.93m, while Poland's Dawid Wegner took third with a personal-best 85.16m.The victory was another chapter in Pathirage's extraordinary 2026 campaign.The 23-year-old has now won 11 of his 12 competitions this year, including his last six. After his Rome explosion, he won in Ostrava and at the Doha Diamond League before creating history in Glasgow as Sri Lanka's first Commonwealth Games javelin champion.He then edged out Chopra at the Lausanne Diamond League, winning with 88.14m, just nine centimetres better than the Indian's 88.05m. That was Chopra's best effort of the season.Chopra, a two-time Olympic medallist, skipped Zurich but still qualified for the Diamond League Final in Brussels as the sixth-ranked thrower. The season-ending showdown on Sept 4-5 now presents another major Pathirage-Chopra clash.And this is a rivalry that could carry even greater weight soon. After Brussels, both stars are set to have the Asian Games on their radar.For Chopra, the challenge is clear: Pathirage is no longer merely a rising contender. With consistency, distance and an extraordinary winning streak behind him, the Sri Lankan has transformed himself into the benchmark.Zurich only strengthened that message and the pressure, increasingly, is on Chopra. Pathirage's emergence has changed the javelin throw landscape, making every meeting with the Indian a potential season-defining contest ahead for both.
Article Summary: Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage produced a breathtaking 92.07m in Zurich. It was his second throw beyond 92m in 2026, following his world-leading 92.62m national record in Rome in June. He is only the fourth javelin thrower in history to cross the 92m mark twice, joining legendary names like Jan Zelezny, Johannes Vetter and Aki Parviainen.

Article Title: Was away physically for those weeks, but present mentally: Sjoerd Marijne
Article Text:
Hockey Women’s Coach Sjoerd Marijne Clears The Air On His Pre-WC Absence

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: It was 2020 and the pandemic had just begun.Sjoerd Marijne, then the coach of the Indian women's hockey team, was in a cab en route to Bengaluru airport, from where he was supposed to fly back to the Netherlands to join his family. But midway through the ride, he changed his mind and returned to the city's Sports Authority of India centre.It was a difficult decision, but Marijne chose to stay. A year later, he led India to a historic fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics.Six years on, Marijne found himself making a very different choice. When he returned to take charge of the Indian women's team for a second stint, he once again had to find a way to combine his commitment to the team with being there for his family. This time, with the World Cup approaching, he chose to spend a few weeks with his family before rejoining the team - a decision that had been agreed upon when he took up the job.But while Marijne was away from the team physically, he remained closely connected with its preparations. He followed every training session and practice match, stayed in touch with the players and conducted video meetings to ensure he remained on top of the process."I saw every training session and every practice match. I saw everything. So I wasn't there in person, but I was there," Marijne told TOI in an exclusive interview after India recorded their best World Cup finish in 52 years. "I had contact with the players and did video meetings with them, so I was on top of the process."Marijne also credited his support staff, as well as the team's strength and conditioning staff, for giving him the confidence that the team was in good hands. "I had very good assistants like Matias Villa. Tim White, who is doing the under-21s, was also there. So, I knew they were in good hands," he said. "There's a lot of leadership in the team and they knew that they had to do well and give the example, so that's why this was possible. "When Marijne re-joined, he found the squad had continued along the same path. "It was all the same. For the girls, it also felt like I hadn't been away. So that is a positive thing," he said.The Dutchman also stressed that while he was away physically, he had never stepped away from his responsibilities as coach. "It wasn't that for a few weeks I wasn't there mentally. I was only not physically there," he said.For Marijne, the experience also highlighted the growing maturity within the group. The players were able to take responsibility, lean on the senior members and stay true to the team's structure and culture even with their coach away from the training ground."The players knew that I was overseeing everything," he said. "The main thing is that it looked like I was away. I was away physically, but for the players it didn't feel like I was away because I was still involved."Perhaps that was the biggest reassurance for Marijne - that the team had developed enough trust and leadership to keep moving in the same direction, even when he wasn't physically there.
Article Summary: Sjoerd Marijne was in a cab en route to Bengaluru airport, from where he was supposed to fly back to the Netherlands to join his family. But midway through the ride, he changed his mind and returned to the city's Sports Authority of India centre. A year later, he led India to a historic fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics.

Article Title: Pat Cummins joins the rallying cry for Imran Khan

Article Title: VVS masterclass will be knowledge sharing
Article Text:
VVS Laxman

Bengaluru: While the Indian cricket team made its Asian Games debut in Hangzhou in 2023, its first appearance at a multi-sport event came at the 1998 Commonwealth Games. In Kuala Lumpur, a star-studded side featuring Sachin Tendulkar, Anil Kumble, VVS Laxman and Harbhajan Singh bowed out in the league phase. Twenty-five years later, Laxman returned to the multi-sport arena, this time as coach, guiding India to gold in Hangzhou.Now, as the Shreyas Iyer-led Indian team prepares to defend its title at Korogi Athletic Park in Aichi Prefecture, Japan beginning with the quarterfinals on Sept 28, Laxman spoke exclusively to TOI of the unique appeal of multi-sport events, India's Asian Games campaign and the experience of being part of the cricket team's journey from its first CWG appearance to maiden Asian Games gold."My first experience of a multi-discipline event was at the 1998 Commonwealth Games. The whole experience of being part of the Indian contingent feels really great, and that kind of experience every young cricketer should get. It's great that I've had that opportunity both as a player and coach," said the head of cricket at the BCCI Centre of Excellence.Recalling the Hangzhou experience, the former batting great said, "Obviously, it's not like your mainstream cricket series or tournaments that we've been part of since we started playing for the country.The Asian Games was a great experience and exposure because not often do we get to visit the Games village, meet a sportsperson from other disciplines, interact with them, see how they train and prepare. A group of us went to support the Indian badminton team, which was fantastic. "India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are the seeded teams making the quarterfinals directly, with Afghanistan, Japan, Nepal, Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman fighting for the other four knockout berths.While India will start favourites, they can ill afford to take the other teams lightly, with Nepal giving them a run for their medal in the previous edition before India won by 23 runs to make the semifinals.India will play a match against Japan and train in Tokyo for three days before heading to the host city. Laxman pointed to the match against Nepal and said, "One thing which we have learnt playing the game is never underestimate your opponent."Beyond the game, Laxman believes it is about knowledge sharing."Given the experience and the exposure the Indian cricketers have, at the end of the match it's also about sharing that experience with players from other countries. After Nepal ran us close in the previous edition of the Asian Games, their coach invited me to talk to the team, which was an opportunity to share knowledge. It's not just me, but that's the way the entire group of players will approach the experience," Laxman stated.
Article Summary: VVS Laxman spoke exclusively to TOI of the unique appeal of multi-sport events. The Indian cricket team made its Asian Games debut in Hangzhou in 2023. India will defend its title at Korogi Athletic Park in Aichi Prefecture, Japan.

Article Title: Grand Chess Tour: ‘Praggnanandhaa refused to settle for second place’
Article Text:
Indian Grandmaster Praggnanandhaa

CHENNAI: It was the middle of the night in India when golden boy R Praggnanandhaa made history in St Louis, USA. As the 21-year-old became the first Indian to win the Grand Chess Tour (GCT), his long-time coach RB Ramesh and second, GM Vaibhav Suri, were wide awake back home.For the two men, sleep had been the last thing on their minds over the past month as they kept a close watch on Pragg’s campaign in St Louis. After his sensational triumph, Pragg was quick to acknowledge the hours they had put in behind the scenes.“A special appreciation to my trainers, Ramesh sir and Vaibhav. Especially Vaibhav, he compromised his sleep schedule for me. Back home, he was chatting with me despite the time difference. Huge credit to him. He was online throughout… it’s like 3 or 4 am back home,” Pragg said after scripting a remarkable comeback.Pragg overturned a six-point deficit on the final day to beat Fabiano Caruana 15-13. He had been in difficult positions several times during the tournament, but Suri felt it was Pragg’s relentless drive and refusal to give up that helped him rise above them — and, in turn, made the trainer’s job easier.“Six points against a player like Fabiano is not the ideal situation to be in. But the best thing about Pragg is that he has a very strong character. It’s very easy to feel, in a situation like that, when you have very slim chances, ‘Maybe it’s not my tournament’, ‘It’s not my day’, ‘I can let this go.’ He did not feel any of that at all.“I could sense it from the way we were communicating, discussing game strategy, match strategy and opening prep. It’s much easier for me and the others around him to put in that effort when you know the person you’re helping is extremely driven and really wants this. Obviously, at this stage, you don’t want to be satisfied with second place or simply being a GCT finalist,” Suri, beaming with pride, told TOI from New Delhi.That mindset has been central to Pragg’s evolution as a player. No longer the precocious kid who announced himself on the world stage, he has grown into a more complete player — one who can hold his own across all three formats. His results this year have been telling.After a disappointing outing at the Candidates in April, Pragg won Norway Chess, followed it up with the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz title, finished runner-up at the Sinquefield Cup and now has the GCT crown.Ramesh, who has guided Pragg since he was a wide-eyed child, feels his protege is now playing with greater confidence, particularly in shorter time controls, which have not always been his strongest suit.“Winning such big events always gives tremendous confidence,” Ramesh told TOI. “I think that is very important. Being consistent across all three formats is not easy. If they do well in one format, they struggle in another. But he has done well in all three. I hope this is just the beginning because he has to do this consistently across all four formats. That won’t be easy because adapting to different time controls is not easy. ”
Article Summary: R Praggnanandhaa is the first Indian to win the Grand Chess Tour. The 21-year- old overturned a six-point deficit on the final day to beat Fabiano Caruana 15-13. His long-time coach RB Ramesh and second, GM Vaibhav Suri, were wide awake back home.

Article Title: 'Mai wicket-taker hoon': Vaibhav Sooryavanshi sends message to 'Ishan bhaiya' ahead of Duleep Trophy semifinal

Fifteen-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has opened up about his bowling spell in East Zone's opening Duleep Trophy 2026 match, saying he always enjoys bowling and joking that captain Ishan Kishan did not know he was a "wicket-taker."Sooryavanshi, who was named East Zone vice-captain for the tournament, made an impact with the ball in the second innings against North East Zone. The left-arm spinner took two wickets in a three-over spell as East Zone completed an innings and 210-run win on Tuesday.Speaking in a video shared by BCCI Domestic, Sooryavanshi said batters enjoy bowling just as much as bowlers enjoy batting."If you ask any batter, they always enjoy bowling. A batter always enjoys bowling and a bowler always enjoys batting equally," Sooryavanshi said.The teenager said Kishan brought him into the attack because East Zone needed a breakthrough, but added that the captain did not know what he was capable of with the ball."Opponent team's wickets weren't falling, so I was asked to bowl two or three overs. Ishan bhaiya felt like he was taking a risk, but he didn't knew that I am a wicket-taker," he added.Sooryavanshi's spell changed the innings quickly.He first dismissed Kishan Lyngdoh, who was caught at deep covers while trying to play an aerial shot.Three balls later, he got left-handed batter Imliwati Lemtur to edge behind, with Kishan taking the catch behind the stumps.The Bihar youngster said he knew he had only three overs to bowl and wanted to make the most of them."I had only one thing in my mind: that even if I take five wickets, I'm only going to get to bowl three overs only. So (the plan) was to bowl as well as I can and target one spot only and finish my spell well.”The Rajasthan Royals batter did not have much success with the bat in the match. He scored eight in East Zone's only innings but said contributing with the ball made up for it."It was a lot of fun because batting didn't go so well in the match. So, contributing with the ball was great. And of course, when a batter takes a wicket, there's no greater enjoyment than that, so it was a lot of fun!" he concluded.Sooryavanshi now has four wickets in First-Class cricket.East Zone have qualified for the Duleep Trophy semi-finals and will face Central Zone at the BCCI Centre of Excellence Ground 2 in Bengaluru. The match starts at 9:30am on Sunday, while the final begins on September 6.
Article Summary: East Zone vice-captain Vaibhav Sooryavanshi took two wickets in a three-over spell. The left-arm spinner helped East Zone complete an innings and 210-run win. He said he always enjoys bowling and joked captain Ishan Kishan did not know he was a "wicket-taker"

Article Title: ‘Second division cricket’: Michael Vaughan brutally mocks Pakistan batting at Lord’s

Pakistan’s struggles in England have deepened after their batting collapsed for 110 in the first innings of the Lord’s Test, prompting a brutal assessment from former England captain Michael Vaughan Pakistan arrived at Lord’s hoping for a response after being beaten by an innings and 53 runs in the opening Test. The return of regular captain Babar Azam had also provided some optimism, but his comeback did little to change the visitors’ fortunes.Babar managed only eight runs, while Abdullah Shafique (5), Shan Masood (1) and Mohammad Rizwan (7) all fell cheaply. Opener Azan Awais offered some resistance with 46, but Pakistan were bowled out for just 110.Vaughan was scathing in his assessment of the Pakistan batting line-up, arguing that England’s bowlers were operating without any real fear of being punished."I'll be brutally honest. The England bowlers aren't being challenged at all. And this Pakistan batting lineup is possibly the easiest batting lineup I've seen in a long time to bowl to. And not only that, I think as a bowler, I think they're all queuing up to bowl because they know there are wickets out there," Vaughan said on the BBC Test Match Special."You're not going to get hurt. There's no batter that's going to hurt them. No one's going to damage their figures, and it's really, 'roll up, roll up, who wants to get the wickets?'," he added.The former England skipper continued his criticism by questioning whether Pakistan’s current batting unit was even of Test-match standard.With England’s bowlers repeatedly finding breakthroughs, Vaughan suggested the visitors had made life remarkably easy for the hosts."I think they all know that Pakistan aren't going to get big scores. So you're only going to be out there for 40 to 50 overs, so you give everything in every spell, you keep going to Joe Root saying, Err, I'll bowl another one.' There are so many wickets out there," said Vaughan.He then made a particularly harsh comparison, suggesting Pakistan’s batting resembled a second-division county side rather than an international Test team."It's so easy. They're still doing a good job, and they're still looking very threatening. And I think this bowling attack, the way they're bowling, will challenge better batting lineups if they continue in this fashion. But this is Pakistan batting. Is it second division county cricket? There's no way that they are batting in any standard to say that, that is a Test match batting lineup," he added.Pakistan’s batting woes have been compounded by the absence of opener Imam-ul-Haq, who did not bat in the first innings after suffering a calf strain while fielding at Lord’s.England capitalised on Pakistan’s collapse to take a commanding position in the Test. The hosts finished the second day on 81/3 in their second innings, extending their overall lead to 261 runs.After Pakistan’s innings ended inside 38 overs, England remain firmly in control of the second Test and have put the visitors under immense pressure to produce a turnaround in the remainder of the match.
Article Summary: Pakistan bowled out for 110 in first innings of second Test at Lord's. Former England skipper Michael Vaughan criticises Pakistan's batting. Vaughan says England's bowlers are not being challenged at all by Pakistan. England lead Pakistan by 261 runs after second day of Test.

Article Title: ‘India messed up big time’: Ex-captain sounds alarm after costly Colombo blunder
Article Text:
India's Captain Shubman Gill with teammates (PTI Photo)

India’s World Test Championship hopes have taken a hit after the Colombo Test ended in a draw, with former India cricketer Krishnamachari Srikkanth warning that the missed opportunity could have serious consequences for their qualification campaign.India appeared well placed to complete a 2-0 series sweep after taking control of the second Test. Sri Lanka began the final day with six wickets down, leaving India needing only four more wickets to seal victory.Instead, the visitors could manage just two wickets as Sonal Dinusha produced a stunning unbeaten century to frustrate India. The Sri Lankan batter remained unbeaten on 133 and stitched together vital partnerships with the lower order, helping the hosts survive and force a draw after following on.The result meant India had to settle for a 1-0 series victory rather than the 2-0 sweep that had looked within reach.The dropped opportunity in Colombo could prove significant in the race for the WTC Final. India remain fifth in the standings, with Sri Lanka sixth, and now have very little room for error across their remaining seven Tests.According to Srikkanth, India may need an almost perfect run from here to stay in control of their qualification hopes."This draw will make it difficult for India to qualify for the WTC final. Even if India wins five or six of the last seven matches, they'll have to depend on other results. It's questionable if India can beat Australia 5-0 at home. If we give rank turners in that series, Australia can also beat India," Srikkanth said on his YouTube channel.India have seven Tests left in their WTC campaign and need to win at least six of them to control their own destiny.A major challenge will come when Australia travel to India. Srikkanth cautioned against assuming that home conditions will guarantee results, particularly if India prepare heavily turning pitches.Srikkanth was particularly critical of India’s failure to close out the Colombo Test after creating a strong position.He also highlighted Dinusha’s contribution, with the Sri Lankan batter producing twin centuries at the Sinhalese Sports Club and playing a decisive role in keeping his team alive on the final day."India messed up big time. Sonal Dinusha was amazing throughout the series. This is where you miss a bowler like Bumrah. You need a finishing bowler like him. Though rain helped Sri Lanka a bit, India should have won the match hands down," said Srikkanth.Dinusha’s unbeaten 133 proved crucial as Sri Lanka survived India’s late push and secured a draw, leaving the visitors with a 1-0 series win but also a potentially costly setback in their WTC campaign.

India appeared well placed to complete a 2-0 series sweep after taking control of the second Test. Sri Lanka began the final day with six wickets down, leaving India needing only four more wickets to seal victory. Article Title: Dewald Brevis’ 75 runs goes in vain as Namibia beat South Africa by 18 runs in tri-series opener
Article Text:
Namibia repeat South Africa upset

Frylinck, Steenkamp provide perfect start

Namibia pacers rattle Proteas

Namibia produced another memorable upset against South Africa, defending 163/9 to secure an 18-run victory in the opening match of the Namibia T20I Tri-Series 2026 at the Namibia Cricket Ground on Friday. It was Namibia's second win over South Africa in 10 months, underlining their growing stature in the shortest format. The hosts appeared to have left the door open after South Africa restricted them to 163, but their bowlers responded brilliantly to dismiss the Proteas for 145/9 in 20 overs.Dewald Brevis produced a superb 75 off 50 balls, but his valiant effort could not take South Africa over the line. Ruben Trumpelmann and JJ Smit claimed three wickets apiece to lead Namibia's bowling attack.Asked to bat first, Namibia made an explosive start through Jan Frylinck and Louren Steenkamp. The opening pair put together an 84-run partnership, giving the hosts the platform they needed to post a competitive total.Frylinck was particularly impressive, striking 60 off 38 balls with six fours and two sixes. Steenkamp complemented him perfectly with a brisk 41 off 29 deliveries. Namibia appeared set for a much bigger total when they reached 133/3 in the 15th over, but South Africa hit back strongly during the final five overs.The Proteas' bowlers suddenly found their rhythm and picked up six wickets for just 30 runs in the final five overs. Prenelan Subrayen led the fightback with 3/32, while captain Bjorn Fortuin bowled a disciplined spell to finish with 2/17.The late collapse prevented Namibia from reaching what could have been a significantly higher score, with the hosts eventually finishing on 163/9. South Africa therefore needed 164 to begin the tri-series with a victory.The chase began poorly for South Africa as Namibia's seamers immediately applied pressure. Trumpelmann was particularly effective, using his left-arm angle to trouble the Proteas' top order. He eventually finished with 3/24, while Smit provided excellent support with 3/31.South Africa's young batting line-up struggled to build partnerships, leaving Brevis with the responsibility of keeping the chase alive. Brevis responded with a magnificent counter-attacking innings.The right-hander scored 75 from 50 balls, including five sixes, and repeatedly found boundaries to keep South Africa within touching distance of the target.With wickets falling around him, Brevis continued to attack and appeared capable of taking the Proteas close to victory. But his dismissal in the 18th over effectively ended South Africa's hopes.Duan Jansen provided a late push with 25 off 17 balls, but Namibia's bowlers held their nerve during the closing overs.With the required rate climbing and wickets running out, South Africa finished on 145/9, 18 runs short of the target.
Article Summary: Namibia beat South Africa by 18 runs in the opening match of the Namibia T20I Tri-Series 2026. It was Namibia's second win over South Africa in 10 months. Jan Frylinck and Louren Steenkamp put on 84 for the first wicket. South Africa were bowled out for 145 in their 20 overs.

NEW DELHI: For Anaya Bangar, the prospect of returning to competitive cricket is about much more than stepping back onto a field. It represents the culmination of a lonely and emotionally difficult journey that began when she started her transition in 2022.Now on the cusp of reclaiming her cricketing life, the 25-year-old trans athlete says Cricket Australia’s decision to provide her a pathway into women’s cricket is a moment she once thought might never arrive.“It’s been lonely, it’s been brutal, but it’s also been worth it,” Anaya told PTI.Her journey eventually culminated in gender-affirming surgery in March this year. In June, she approached Cricket Australia’s Head of Integrity Jacqui Partridge after learning about the governing body’s policy for transgender and gender-diverse players. The process eventually resulted in CA clearing Anaya for a pathway towards competitive women’s cricket, subject to the policy’s eligibility requirements.“Right now, just hearing the news about Cricket Australia clearing me, and basically providing me a path to play women's cricket, to play cricket as who I am is huge for me,” she said.Anaya admitted that the transition was an extremely difficult period, particularly while navigating the challenges of being a trans athlete in the current political climate.“...when you're transitioning, and when you're a trans-athlete, during this political climate in this world, it can get very isolating. You feel very lonely, you feel like there's no one who really understands out there,” she said.She found that solitude helped her deal with a situation in which she often felt others were trying to tell her what was best for her.“Everyone out there is trying to give you solutions, when you know that your own case is the right one. You know what is happening with you is injustice. So, during all of this, just the fact of being with myself, solitude has helped me a lot throughout all this,” she added.Anaya, whose father is former India player and decorated coach Sanjay Bangar , said she had eventually given up hope of playing cricket again after beginning her transition.“To be honest, emotionally, it's just been all by myself, but I'm grateful for the support for the necessities that I had from my family,” she said.“I never thought that I'll be able to get (to) play cricket ever since the day I started transitioning. I just tried to put myself out there and see what happens, and whatever works, works. And throughout all this, I think the universe has backed me a lot, and here we are,” she added.Anaya said the experience of stepping away from the sport she loved, undergoing major personal changes and dealing with changing family dynamics ultimately made her stronger.“To be honest, transitioning was always about being happy and comfortable in my own skin. And I had to take the necessary steps during that time in my life to basically give up the sport that I loved. Go through major changes, go through major family dynamic changes and everything,” she said.“...And I couldn't be more grateful for this journey. It's been a rollercoaster, it's been brutal, it's been filled with emotions, but I'm glad I'm on the stepping stone now.”
Article Summary: Anaya Bangar, 25, started her transition in 2022 and underwent gender-affirming surgery in March this year. In June, she approached Cricket Australia’s Head of Integrity Jacqui Partridge after learning about the governing body's policy for transgender and gender-diverse players. The process eventually resulted in CA clearing Anaya for a pathway towards competitive women's cricket, subject to the policy's eligibility requirements.

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.
